lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So does psychology actually prove what it says it proves?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: That's the big worry in Estimating the reproducibility of psychological Science. The authors worried that many findings might not hold up when tested again.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Half the magnitude? What does that even mean?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Think of it like measuring a force. If the original study said the push was five units, and the new one says only two and a half, the effect is much weaker than advertised.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: And how many studies did they actually check to know this?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: They looked at one hundred experimental and correlational studies from three top psychology journals. They made sure to use fresh materials whenever possible.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Did they just copy the old test exactly or make new versions?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: They used high-powered designs meaning large sample sizes, and they grabbed original materials when those were available to keep things as true as possible.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So ninety-seven percent of the originals worked. What about their new ones?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Only thirty-six percent of those replications showed statistically significant results. That is a huge drop compared to the original findings.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: Why did so many original studies get such good results in the first place?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Ninety-seven percent of those original studies had statistically significant results, which suggests some papers might have been lucky or had hidden bias.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: What about the numbers on the charts in the new study?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Forty-seven percent of the original effect sizes fell inside the ninety-five percent confidence interval of the replication result. That means most effects were weaker than claimed.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: And what did people who looked at these results say?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Thirty-nine percent of effects were subjectively rated by experts to have successfully replicated the original finding. That rating was lower than the raw numbers suggest.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So if we mix both sets of data together, does it help?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: If we assume no bias in the original results and combine them, only sixty-eight percent would still have statistically significant effects overall.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So the team quality didn't matter much? What did actually predict success?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Correlational tests showed replication success was better predicted by how strong the original evidence was than by who ran the study.

lines.speaker: Juniper
lines.text: So until more data comes in, we probably can't trust most psychology findings right now.
